_meta.note: Additive entries are derived from additives_risk.json (risk_tier + safety + sources copied verbatim). Do not hand-edit; run the script.

entries.why_used: Helps food keep longer by slowing spoilage from microbes.

entries.why_used: Helps food keep longer by slowing spoilage from microbes.
entries.safety: Preservative with an EFSA group ADI; intake by children who consume many soft drinks can approach the ADI, and benzene can form in some drinks that also contain vitamin C.
misconceptions: The benzene concern applies only to some drinks that also contain vitamin C, not to sodium benzoate in general

entries.what: Sulphur dioxide, a preservative and antioxidant.
entries.why_used: Helps food keep longer by slowing spoilage from microbes.
entries.safety: EFSA's 2022 re-evaluation could not confirm the safety of the previous ADI due to data gaps, and some people are sensitive to sulphites; it must be declared as an allergen in the EU and US.
who_should_avoid: people who are sensitive to sulphites, including some people with asthma

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of sulphur dioxide and sulphites (E220-E228), 2022

entries.what: A curing salt (potassium nitrite) for processed meats.
entries.why_used: Helps food keep longer by slowing spoilage from microbes.
entries.safety: Curing salt for processed meats; EFSA's 2023 assessment found dietary exposure to nitrosamines, which can form from nitrites, raises a health concern across age groups.

sources.name: EFSA opinion on nitrosamines in food, 2023

entries.what: A curing salt (sodium nitrite) for processed meats.

entries.safety: Curing salt for processed meats; EFSA's 2023 assessment found dietary exposure to nitrosamines, which can form from nitrites, raises a health concern, and the EU tightened permitted levels in 2023.

sources.name: EFSA opinion on nitrosamines in food, 2023
EU Regulation 2023/2108 (lower limits for nitrites and nitrates)

entries.why_used: Helps food keep longer by slowing spoilage from microbes.

EU Regulation 2023/2108 (lower limits for nitrites and nitrates)

entries.what: A sweetener used in place of some or all sugar.
entries.why_used: Adds sweetness with little or no sugar and few or no calories.
entries.safety: Sweetener with an EFSA ADI that typical intakes stay within; the WHO's 2023 guideline advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners for weight management.
misconceptions: Regulators set an intake limit that typical use stays within; the WHO advice is about relying on sweeteners for weight loss, not about safety at normal intakes

entries.what: A sweetener used in place of some or all sugar.
entries.why_used: Adds sweetness with little or no sugar and few or no calories.
entries.safety: EFSA and JECFA maintain an ADI that typical intakes stay well within; IARC classified it Group 2B (limited evidence) in 2023, which JECFA reviewed without changing the ADI.
who_should_avoid: people with phenylketonuria (PKU), because it contains phenylalanine
misconceptions: At normal intakes it has not been shown to cause the health harms sometimes claimed online

sources.name: EFSA full risk assessment of aspartame, 2013

entries.what: A sweetener used in place of some or all sugar.
entries.why_used: Adds sweetness with little or no sugar and few or no calories.
entries.safety: Sweetener with a JECFA/EFSA ADI that typical intakes stay within; the WHO's 2023 guideline advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners for weight management and EFSA re-evaluation is ongoing.
misconceptions: The WHO advice is about using sweeteners for weight management, not a finding that normal intakes are harmful

entries.what: Hen's egg or a part of it.
entries.why_used: Binds, sets, and adds structure, richness, and colour.
entries.safety: Eggs are a safe, nutritious food for most people; they are a common allergen.
who_should_avoid: people with an egg allergy

entries.what: A liquid sugar made from starch, such as maize or wheat.
entries.why_used: Adds sweetness, texture, and shelf life and stops crystals forming.
entries.safety: Glucose syrup is a form of sugar; the WHO advice on limiting free sugars applies to it.
who_should_avoid: people managing diabetes may want to watch total sugars

sources.name: WHO guideline: sugars intake for adults and children, 2015

entries.what: A liquid sweetener made from corn starch with some glucose converted to fructose.
entries.why_used: A cheap liquid sweetener that adds sweetness and shelf life, common in drinks.
entries.safety: It is a form of sugar; the WHO advice on limiting free sugars applies to it as to other sugars.
who_should_avoid: people managing diabetes may want to watch total sugars
misconceptions: The evidence treats it much like other added sugars; the concern is total added sugar, not this syrup uniquely

sources.name: WHO guideline: sugars intake for adults and children, 2015

entries.what: A natural sweetener made by bees.
entries.why_used: Adds sweetness and flavour.
entries.safety: Honey is a form of sugar and safe for most people; it should not be given to infants under 12 months.
who_should_avoid: infants under 12 months
people managing diabetes may want to watch total sugars
misconceptions: Honey is still a sugar nutritionally, even though it is less processed than table sugar

entries.why_used: Thickens sauces and adds structure or a light texture.
entries.safety: Maize starch is a safe, common food ingredient.

entries.why_used: Adds flavour, protein, and richness.
entries.safety: Milk is a safe, nutritious food for most people; it is a common allergen and contains lactose.
who_should_avoid: people with a milk allergy
people with lactose intolerance

entries.what: A cereal grain, often rolled into flakes.
entries.why_used: A staple grain used in cereals and baking; a source of fibre.
entries.safety: Oats are a safe whole grain and a source of dietary fibre.
who_should_avoid: some people with coeliac disease react to oats unless they are certified gluten-free

entries.why_used: Used for cooking and dressings and for its flavour.
entries.safety: Olive oil is safe to eat and is rich in unsaturated fat.

entries.what: A vegetable oil pressed from the fruit of the oil palm.
entries.why_used: Gives a smooth texture and long shelf life and stays solid at room temperature.
entries.safety: Palm oil is safe to eat; it is high in saturated fat, which health bodies suggest limiting to support heart health.
who_should_avoid: people advised to limit saturated fat
misconceptions: Concerns about palm oil centre on saturated fat and the environment, not on it being unsafe to eat

sources.name: WHO guideline: saturated and trans-fatty acid intake, 2023

entries.what: A vegetable oil pressed from rapeseed (canola).
entries.why_used: A neutral cooking oil used for frying, baking, and dressings.
entries.safety: Rapeseed (canola) oil is safe to eat and is low in saturated fat.

entries.what: A cereal grain, sometimes milled into flour.
entries.why_used: A staple carbohydrate; rice flour adds structure in gluten-free foods.
entries.safety: Rice is a safe, widely eaten staple grain.

entries.what: Sodium chloride — the mineral we know as table salt.
entries.why_used: Adds flavour and, in many foods, helps preserve them and shape texture.
entries.safety: Salt is safe, but most people eat more sodium than health bodies suggest; the WHO recommends limiting sodium to help manage blood pressure.
who_should_avoid: people advised to limit sodium, for example for high blood pressure
misconceptions: Sea salt and pink salt are still mostly sodium chloride, like ordinary table salt

sources.name: WHO guideline: sodium intake for adults and children, 2012

entries.what: Milk with the fat and water removed, dried to a powder.
entries.why_used: Adds dairy solids, protein, and body without adding liquid.
entries.safety: Skimmed milk powder is safe for most people; it is a milk product and a common allergen.
who_should_avoid: people with a milk allergy
people with lactose intolerance

entries.what: Sugar (mostly sucrose) that adds sweetness and energy.
entries.why_used: Adds sweetness and bulk, helps browning, and can help preserve foods like jam.
entries.safety: Sugar is safe as a food; the WHO suggests keeping free sugars below 10% of daily energy, and ideally 5%, mainly to protect teeth and help manage weight.
who_should_avoid: people managing diabetes may want to watch total sugars
misconceptions: The health guidance is about how much sugar we eat, not that any sugar is harmful in itself

sources.name: WHO guideline: sugars intake for adults and children, 2015

entries.what: A vegetable oil pressed from sunflower seeds.
entries.why_used: Used for frying, texture, and as a neutral-tasting fat.
entries.safety: Sunflower oil is safe to eat and is mostly unsaturated fat.

entries.why_used: Acts as a base or carrier and adjusts consistency.
entries.safety: Water is an essential nutrient with no intake concern in food.

entries.why_used: Forms the structure of breads, baked goods, and batters.
entries.safety: Wheat flour is safe for most people; it contains gluten and is a common allergen.
who_should_avoid: people with coeliac disease or a wheat allergy
people avoiding gluten

entries.what: The protein-rich liquid left when milk is made into cheese, often dried.
entries.why_used: Adds protein, flavour, and texture.
entries.safety: Whey is safe for most people; it is a milk product and a common allergen.
who_should_avoid: people with a milk allergy

entries.what: A microorganism used to leaven bread and in fermentation.
entries.why_used: Makes dough rise and adds flavour.
entries.safety: Baker's yeast is a safe, common food ingredient.
